strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: when stochastic steepest descent preserves the norm-induced max-margin behavior of full-batch methods. The unified treatment of entry-wise and Schatten norms connects normalized SGD, SignSGD, and idealized spectral descent.

Originality: The random-reshuffling momentum analysis and variance-reduction guarantees provide meaningful extensions of the cited full-batch work. Lemma C.10's global gradient-stability bound offers a concrete route to removing explicit dimension factors.

Soundness: The orthogonal-data analysis in Theorem 4.9 gives an interpretable example of scale-independent, class-frequency-dependent bias. The variance-reduction analysis also identifies a useful mechanism: estimator error becomes proportional to the shrinking step size, permitting exact margin recovery.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript supplies algorithm pseudocode, extensive derivations, and synthetic illustrations across three geometries. It appropriately acknowledges the restrictions to separable linear classification and specially constructed data. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: The advertised large-batch stochastic result has no non-full-batch regime under the stated assumptions. Lemma C.1 implies that every unit-norm W has entries bounded by 1, so every sample margin is at most 2||x_i||_1 and hence gamma <= 2R. Since Section 3 requires n = mb with integer m, every non-full batch has m >= 2. Consequently, Theorem 4.1's effective margin satisfies rho = gamma - 4(m-1)R <= -2R. Its positivity condition therefore permits only b = n. This is more consequential than a conservative condition: the first headline contribution does not establish any genuinely mini-batch guarantee.

The central interpretation exceeds the mathematical statements. Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 provide one-sided bounds implying liminf of the normalized margin is at least rho; they do not establish convergence of the direction or identify rho as the limiting margin. Likewise, a sufficient large-batch condition does not establish that convergence occurs 'only' with large batches. For non-strictly convex norms, Theorem 4.6's convergence of the margin to gamma does not establish convergence to the same particular parameter direction as full-batch training. These distinctions affect the abstract, contribution statements, and conclusions.

The claimed slowdown from momentum and variance reduction is not established by comparing upper bounds. Larger prefactors in conservative bounds do not demonstrate slower actual convergence, and the iteration-rate exponent remains unchanged for a fixed learning-rate schedule. No matching lower bounds or controlled rate measurements establish the proposed intrinsic trade-off. Computational comparisons should also account for variance reduction's full-gradient snapshot and additional gradient evaluations.

The momentum condition is extremely restrictive, and the experiments do not validate its guaranteed regime. Theorem 4.3 requires 1-beta_1 < gamma/[2Rm(m^2-1)], scaling at best as m^-3. In the reported mini-batch experiments, m = 10 and beta_1 = 0.99 give rho = gamma - 19.8R < 0 because gamma <= 2R. Thus even the highest tested momentum lies outside the theorem's applicability. The empirical behavior is interesting, but it does not substantiate the quantitative batch-momentum guarantee.

Lemma H.1 incorrectly equates the spectral and Frobenius argmax sets for rank-one gradients. For G = diag(1,0), both diag(1,0) and diag(1,1) maximize alignment over the spectral unit ball, whereas only diag(1,0) does so over the Frobenius unit ball. Equivalence holds for a specified rank-one polar-factor selection, not every maximizer, contrary to the unrestricted selection statement in Section 3. The algorithm definition and scope of the equivalence need correction.

Experimental reproducibility and presentation need improvement. Section 5 describes Gaussian features as linearly separable without specifying the label-generation or class-conditional construction that ensures separability. It omits the max-margin solver and tolerances, random seeds, and variability across runs; Appendix J does not specify its class probabilities or scale ranges. Cosine similarity to one optimizer-selected solution is also inconclusive when the max-margin solution is nonunique. Figures 3 and 4 incorrectly describe their geometry as the l2 norm, and the many small panels make quantitative assessment difficult.

strengths: Originality: The unified treatment of random-reshuffling steepest descent across entry-wise and Schatten norms addresses a meaningful extension of full-batch implicit-bias theory. Analyzing momentum and variance reduction together provides useful new understanding beyond proposing another optimizer.

Technical merit: Lemma C.10 gives a useful gradient-stability bound without an explicit dimension factor, and Lemma C.12 exploits epoch-wise cancellation to control momentum sampling error. The variance-reduction analysis offers a substantive route to optimal-margin guarantees for arbitrary batch sizes.

Significance: Theorem 4.9 provides an interpretable example where per-sample normalization removes feature-scale information and makes the limiting direction depend on class frequencies. This helps explain why stochastic and full-batch methods can select different solutions.

Presentation and research practice: The algorithm, assumptions, and extensive supporting proofs are provided. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges linear separability and the specialized counterexample; these restrictions are reasonable for theoretical work. No material research-ethics concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness and significance—Theorem 4.1 has no genuinely mini-batch regime under the stated setup. Lemma C.1 implies that every feasible unit-norm W has maximum entry magnitude at most 1, so Assumption 3.2 gives γ ≤ 2R. Since Section 3.1 requires m = n/b to be an integer, any non-full batch has m ≥ 2 and therefore ρ = γ − 4(m−1)R ≤ −2R < 0. Consequently, the theorem applies only to b = n. This invalidates the advertised contribution of a nontrivial large-batch approximation gap; the issue is stronger than a merely conservative sufficient condition.

Soundness—The manuscript repeatedly overinterprets margin bounds as directional convergence. Theorem 4.3 establishes a lower bound on the limiting inferior of the normalized margin, not convergence of the direction or equality of the limiting margin to ρ. Theorem 4.6 establishes optimal-margin convergence, but without uniqueness it does not establish convergence to the same particular full-batch solution or trajectory. These distinctions matter especially for the non-strictly-convex norms explicitly covered.

Soundness—Claims that momentum and variance reduction slow convergence are not established by larger upper-bound constants. The displayed rates retain the same iteration exponent for fixed algorithmic parameters; no matching lower bounds or controlled computational comparisons establish an actual slowdown. Likewise, a sufficient large-batch condition and a specialized per-sample counterexample do not justify the abstract's assertion that convergence without momentum occurs only with large batches.

Evaluation—The small-batch momentum experiments do not satisfy the theorem's condition. With n = 200, b = 20, and β1 = 0.99, Theorem 4.3 gives ρ = γ − 19.8R < 0 because γ ≤ 2R. The plots can illustrate behavior beyond the guarantee, but they do not validate the stated positive-effective-margin regime. Experiments should report γ/R, include admissible momentum settings, and distinguish finite-time improvement from exact asymptotic recovery.

Reproducibility—Section 5 specifies Gaussian features and balanced labels but does not explain their construction sufficiently to ensure the asserted linear separability. The manuscript also omits the max-margin solver and tolerances, random seeds, repeated-run uncertainty, and an implementation link. Appendix J leaves the class-specific scale ranges and multinomial probabilities unspecified. Cosine similarity to a single numerical optimizer also requires care when the max-margin solution is nonunique.

Presentation—The high-level organization is clear, but inaccurate claims recur in the abstract, theorem interpretations, and conclusion. Figures 3 and 4 incorrectly identify their geometries as ℓ2, and the small multi-panel plots are difficult to inspect. The useful momentum, variance-reduction, and counterexample results need a substantially more precise statement of what is proved before the contribution can be reliably built upon.

strengths: Originality: The unified treatment of random reshuffling, momentum, and variance reduction across entry-wise and Schatten-p geometries extends the cited full-batch analyses in a useful direction. Explicit batch–momentum dependence is a meaningful theoretical objective.

Soundness: Lemma C.10 provides a useful gradient-stability bound using the global entry-wise ℓ1 norm. The epoch-wise cancellation argument and variance-reduction analysis offer substantive mechanisms for controlling gradient-direction error.

Significance: Theorem 4.6's recovery of the optimal margin through variance reduction for arbitrary batch sizes is potentially valuable. The orthogonal-data construction also clearly illustrates how per-sample normalization can discard sample-scale information and introduce frequency-dependent bias.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript supplies algorithm pseudocode and extensive proofs, and organizes the different algorithmic regimes clearly. It appropriately acknowledges the restriction to separable linear models and the specialized counterexample. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Decisive scope issue in Theorem 4.1: Its purported large-mini-batch regime contains only full-batch training under the stated assumptions. Lemma C.1 gives ∥W∥max ≤ ∥W∥, so every feasible unit-norm classifier has pairwise margins at most 2R, implying γ ≤ 2R. Since m = n/b is an integer, any genuine mini-batch setting has m ≥ 2 and therefore ρ = γ − 4(m−1)R ≤ −2R < 0. Thus the theorem establishes no nontrivial mini-batch guarantee, undermining a headline contribution. This is more substantial than merely having a conservative threshold.

The claims exceed the mathematical conclusions. Theorems 4.1 and 4.3 provide one-sided lower bounds on normalized margin, implying a liminf of at least ρ; they do not establish convergence of the direction or identify the limiting margin as ρ. Likewise, optimal-margin convergence in Theorem 4.6 does not by itself identify a unique limiting classifier for non-strictly-convex norms. Statements that convergence occurs 'only' with large batches also turn a sufficient condition into an unsupported necessity claim.

The claimed convergence slowdown from momentum or variance reduction is not established. The corollaries give larger upper-bound constants while retaining the same iteration exponent for fixed algorithmic parameters. Comparing these upper bounds does not prove that the actual algorithms converge more slowly. The abstract and explanatory discussion should distinguish conservative guarantees from intrinsic algorithmic trade-offs.

The momentum guarantee is extremely restrictive and the experiments do not test its certified regime. Theorem 4.3 requires 1−β1 < γ/[2Rm(m²−1)]. For the experimental m = 10, γ ≤ 2R implies β1 > 0.99899 as a necessary condition for this theorem to apply; even the largest tested value, 0.99, fails it. The experiments illustrate behavior outside the guarantee but cannot validate the stated quantitative batch–momentum trade-off.

Lemma H.1 incorrectly equates the spectral-norm and Frobenius-norm argmax sets. For a rank-one gradient uvᵀ, spectral maximizers can include uvᵀ plus orthogonal components with operator norm at most one, whereas the Frobenius maximizer is uniquely uvᵀ. The claimed equivalence needs an explicit rank-one selection convention, particularly because Section 3 states that results accommodate arbitrary maximizers.

Experimental reproducibility and presentation need improvement. Section 5 specifies Gaussian features but does not explain how labels or class means ensure separability. The manuscript omits the max-margin solver and tolerances, seed variability, and precise class-specific scale ranges in Appendix J. Figures 3 and 4 incorrectly describe their geometry as ℓ2. These omissions limit independent verification, especially when cosine similarity is measured against potentially nonunique max-margin solutions.

strengths: Originality and significance: The unified treatment of random-reshuffling steepest descent across entry-wise and Schatten norms is useful. Extending the analysis beyond Signum to include momentum and SVRG-style corrections provides meaningful new understanding of stochastic implicit bias.

Soundness: The central proof mechanisms are well motivated: epoch-wise cancellation controls momentum noise (Lemma C.12), while snapshot corrections make the gradient error vanish relative to the loss proxy (Lemma C.13). The variance-reduction result establishes recovery of the optimal margin without the positive-effective-margin restriction required by ordinary momentum.

The counterexample in Proposition 4.2 is explicit and convincing. Theorem 4.10 also supplies an analytically tractable example showing how per-sample normalization can replace sensitivity to sample scale with sensitivity to class frequency.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript provides algorithm pseudocode, extensive proofs, and a useful explanation of the dimension-free gradient-stability improvement. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges linear separability and the specialized per-sample construction. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent from the synthetic and MNIST experiments.
weaknesses: The claimed characterization of limiting behavior exceeds the momentum theorem. Theorem 4.4 establishes liminf of the normalized margin at least rho; it does not establish convergence of the margin to rho or convergence of the parameter direction to an approximate max-margin solution. Likewise, attaining the optimal margin in Theorem 4.7 does not generally identify the same particular solution or trajectory as full-batch training when maximizers are nonunique. These distinctions matter for the paper's central implicit-bias claims.

The claimed slowdown from momentum and variance reduction is not established by comparing upper bounds. Larger prefactors or sufficient transient thresholds do not prove slower actual convergence or an unavoidable trade-off, and the displayed rates retain the same iteration exponents. No matching lower bounds or targeted computational comparisons establish this interpretation. The abstract and discussion should consistently describe more conservative guarantees.

The momentum condition is highly restrictive and is not tested in the main mini-batch experiment. With n = 200 and b = 20, m = 10; at beta = 0.99, Theorem 4.4 gives rho = gamma - 19.8R < 0 because gamma <= 2R. Thus even the largest tested momentum does not satisfy the theorem. The experiments illustrate qualitative behavior but do not validate the stated batch-momentum guarantee or its quantitative dependence.

The advertised fully explicit parameter dependence is incomplete. In Corollary E.5, the transient calculation suppresses dependence on rho: the polynomial stability threshold depends on the noise constant divided by rho, and Lemma E.2 introduces another inverse-rho dependence. Since rho itself depends on batch size and momentum and can approach zero, the displayed rates do not transparently characterize that trade-off uniformly.

Experimental reproducibility is insufficient. Section 5 does not explain how the stated Gaussian features and prescribed class counts produce separable data, and it omits the max-margin solver, tolerances, seeds, and variability across runs. Appendix K.1 supplies plots without a complete MNIST training configuration. Cosine similarity to one selected optimizer is also an unreliable diagnostic of max-margin recovery for norms with nonunique solutions.

The nonlinear experiment provides limited support for the conclusions. Its sigmoid network lies outside the theory, and the proposed normalization by the maximum of the two layer norms is not a scale-invariant margin for this model. Figure 5 shows qualitative training behavior without establishing optimal-margin recovery. More generally, the strongest positive results concern margin guarantees in separable linear classification, so the broader optimizer and language-model motivation should be calibrated accordingly.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful question: when does stochastic normalized steepest descent preserve full-batch max-margin behavior? The variance-reduction result in Theorem 4.7 is particularly valuable because it guarantees optimal normalized margins for arbitrary batch sizes.

Originality: The unified treatment of entry-wise and Schatten norms, random reshuffling, momentum, and variance reduction extends the narrower settings discussed in prior work. Lemma C.10 provides a useful gradient-stability bound without an explicit dimension factor under the stated data normalization.

Soundness: Proposition 4.2 gives a clear, verifiable SignSGD counterexample. Theorem 4.10 also provides an informative explicit example in which sample frequencies, rather than sample scales, determine the limiting direction.

Presentation and reproducibility: The algorithm, assumptions, and extensive derivations make the approach inspectable. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges linear separability and the specialized per-sample construction. I see no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: Soundness of the central interpretation: Theorem 4.4 establishes an eventual margin lower bound, liminf margin ≥ ρ, rather than convergence of the direction or convergence of the margin to ρ. Similarly, Theorem 4.7 establishes convergence to the optimal margin value, not necessarily to the same particular solution or trajectory as full-batch descent when maximizers are nonunique. Statements about recovering the full-batch solution and trajectory exceed these guarantees.

The claimed slowdown is not established. Sections 4.2–4.3 and the abstract interpret larger upper-bound coefficients as showing that momentum or variance reduction slows convergence. Comparing upper bounds does not establish an actual ordering of convergence speeds; the time exponents are also unchanged. No matching lower bounds or controlled rate experiments substantiate this central trade-off, although some passages correctly describe the bounds as merely more conservative.

The explicit batch–momentum rate dependence needs qualification. Appendix E.5 absorbs dependence on ρ into constants even though ρ = γ − 2(1−β1)m(m²−1)R itself depends on both parameters. The transient conditions involve inverse powers of ρ and deteriorate near ρ = 0. Corollary 4.6 therefore does not transparently capture the advertised parameter trade-off unless a uniform positive lower bound on ρ is imposed.

The experiments do not validate the quantitative momentum condition. For the principal mini-batch setting, m = 200/20 = 10 and β1 = 0.99, Theorem 4.4 requires ρ = γ − 19.8R > 0, which is impossible given the paper's own γ ≤ 2R bound. These experiments illustrate behavior outside the guarantee, but do not establish its tightness or the predicted parameter dependence. The nonlinear sigmoid-network experiment is likewise illustrative rather than a test of the linear max-margin theorem.

Some proof steps require correction before the finite-time bounds are fully reliable as written. On pages 43 and 52, the normalized-gap derivation replaces the denominator ||Wt|| by the cumulative step size using only an upper bound on ||Wt||; that substitution does not follow in the displayed ratio. A corrected argument using positivity of the unnormalized margin appears possible. Lemma E.2 also states a threshold with a factor of two less than its proof derives.

Experimental reproducibility is incomplete. Section 5 does not explain how the Gaussian features and labels are constructed to ensure separability, how reference max-margin solutions are computed, or solver tolerances. Seeds, repetitions, and uncertainty estimates are absent. Appendix K adds little implementation detail for MNIST, and iteration-based comparisons do not account for the full-gradient snapshot cost of variance reduction.

Overall, the theoretical framework has clear merits, but unsupported convergence and slowdown interpretations, incomplete parameter accounting, and insufficient quantitative validation outweigh them in the current submission. A revised paper that states the narrower guarantees precisely and validates their parameter dependence would be substantially stronger.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a useful gap between full-batch implicit-bias theory and stochastic normalized optimization. Its joint treatment of batch size, momentum, and variance reduction across entry-wise and Schatten norms is relevant to understanding SignSGD and spectral descent.

Originality: The random-reshuffling momentum analysis and the recovery of the optimal margin through variance reduction are meaningful extensions of the cited full-batch and fixed-cycle results. Lemmas C.10–C.13 provide a coherent mechanism connecting gradient stability, epoch-wise cancellation, and margin growth.

Soundness: Proposition 4.2 gives a clear, verifiable failure example for per-sample SignSGD. Theorem 4.10 also provides an informative explicit characterization on orthogonal data, showing how class frequency can replace sample hardness in determining the limiting direction.

Presentation and limitations: The manuscript clearly separates the algorithmic settings, supplies pseudocode and extensive derivations, and acknowledges the restrictions to separable linear models and specially constructed per-sample examples. These restrictions are reasonable for theoretical work. No material research-ethics concerns are apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness of the claimed implicit-bias characterization: Theorem 4.4 establishes an asymptotic lower bound on normalized margin, namely liminf margin ≥ ρ. It does not establish convergence of the margin or parameter direction to an approximate max-margin solution. Likewise, optimal-margin convergence in Theorem 4.7 does not establish convergence to the same particular full-batch solution when the norm permits nonunique maximizers. Claims about recovering the full-batch trajectory are stronger still and are unsupported by the stated results.

The claimed slowdown is not established. Larger upper-bound constants do not prove that momentum or variance reduction slows convergence, and the displayed rates retain the same dependence on iteration count. Comparing convergence toward ρ with convergence toward γ also compares different targets. The abstract and Sections 4.2–4.3 should distinguish conservative guarantees from an intrinsic speed-versus-bias trade-off, or supply matching lower bounds.

The advertised explicit batch–momentum rates conceal important dependence on the effective margin. Lemma E.2 contains 1/ρ, and the stability threshold requires α1ηt ≤ ρ/4. However, the derivation of Corollary E.5 treats these factors as constants; Step 2 even substitutes γ for ρ. Since ρ itself depends on batch size and momentum and can approach zero, the displayed parameter dependence is not uniform under the stated condition ρ > 0. A quantitative lower bound on ρ or explicit dependence on it is needed.

The experiments do not validate the sufficient momentum condition quantitatively. For n = 200, b = 20, and β1 = 0.99, Theorem 4.4 gives ρ = γ − 19.8R < 0 because γ ≤ 2R. Thus even the strongest mini-batch momentum setting shown lies outside the theorem's guarantee. The empirical trends are useful, but a sweep relating measured margins to the guaranteed regime would better substantiate the central trade-off.

Algorithm specification needs clarification at nonunique steepest-descent solutions. Section 3 states that results hold for any maximizer, but Appendix H.1's exact equivalence between per-sample spectral descent and normalized SGD requires choosing the rank-one polar factor. For a rank-one gradient, additional components on orthogonal singular subspaces can also maximize the spectral-norm-constrained objective. The relevant selection convention should be stated explicitly.

Empirical reproducibility is incomplete. The Gaussian synthetic-data description does not specify how labels or class means ensure separability; the max-margin solver and its tolerances, random seeds, and variation across runs are unspecified. Appendix K provides MNIST plots without a complete training configuration. Its sigmoid-network margin is also not a scale-invariant counterpart of the linear margin, so this experiment supplies qualitative evidence rather than validation of the theoretical bias.
